title: Chapter 115 — The Pequod Meets The Bachelor
paragraphs: And jolly enough were the sights and sounds that came bearing down before the wind, some few weeks after Ahab's harpoon had been welded.

It was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just wedged in her last cask of oil and bolted down her bursting hatches; and now, in glad holiday dress, was joyously, though somewhat vainly, sailing round among the widely-separated ships on the ground, before turning her prow for home.

The three men at her mastheads wore long streamers of narrow red bunting at their hats; from the stern, a whaleboat was suspended bottom-down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was the long lower jaw of the last whale they had killed. Signals, flags, and jacks of all colors were flying from her rigging on every side. On the forecastle was a great cask lying upon its side, with one head knocked out, and a brimming bright barrel standing within it.

As was afterward learned, the Bachelor had met with the most surprising success — all the more wonderful because, while cruising in the same seas, numerous other vessels had gone entire months without securing a single fish. Not only had barrels of beef and bread been given away to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but additional supplemental casks had been bartered for from the ships she had met.

As this glad ship of good luck bore down upon the moody Pequod, the barbaric sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle; and drawing still nearer, a crowd of her men were seen standing round her huge try-pots, which, covered with the parchment-like stomach-skin of the black-fish, gave forth a loud, drum-like sound as they were pounded upon.

Lord and master over all this scene, the captain stood erect on the ship's elevated quarter-deck, so that the whole rejoicing drama was full before him, and seemed merely staged for his own individual amusement.

And Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black, with a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other's wakes — one all celebrations for things past, the other all forebodings for things to come — their two captains in themselves embodied the whole striking contrast of the scene.
"Come aboard, come aboard!" cried the gay Bachelor's commander, lifting a glass and a bottle in the air.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" gritted Ahab in reply.
"No; only heard of him; but don't believe in him at all," said the other good-humoredly. "Come aboard!"
"You are too damned jolly. Sail on. Have you lost any men?"

"Not enough to speak of — two islanders, that's all; but come aboard, old hearty, come along. I'll soon take that black from your brow. Come along, will you — merry's the play — a full ship and homeward-bound."

"How wondrous familiar is a fool!" muttered Ahab; then aloud: "You are a full ship and homeward-bound, you say; well, then, call me an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go your ways, and I will mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!"

And thus, while the one ship went cheerily before the breeze, the other stubbornly fought against it; and so the two vessels parted; the crew of the Pequod looking with grave, lingering glances toward the receding Bachelor; but the Bachelor's men never heeding their gaze for the lively celebrations they were engaged in.
